lessons.title: Ordering Coffee and Tea

phrases.english: What would you like to drink? (to a man)
phrases.search_term: waiter asking customer at a cafe

phrases.english: What would you like to drink? (to a woman)

reply.english: Sure, I'll bring it to you now.

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.english: Hello, what would you like to drink?

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.english: Hi, do you have coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، شو بتحبها، مظبوطة ولا سادة؟
dialogue.transliteration: akiid, shoo bte7ebba, mazbuu6a walla saada?
dialogue.english: Sure, how do you like it, medium-sweet or plain?

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.english: Medium-sweet, please.

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.english: Okay. One medium-sweet coming up.

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.english: Is there sugar on the table?

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.english: No, I'll bring it to you now.

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.english: Thank you (lit. may God give you health).

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.english: Here you go, your coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Kareem
dialogue.english: Thank you so much, it's really good.

dialogue.speaker: Nadeen
dialogue.english: Enjoy (lit. two healths).

pair.english: What would you like to drink?

response.english: Mint tea, if there is any.

pair.english: Do you like it sweet or plain?

lessons.culture: Damascene coffee is almost always offered as a first gesture of hospitality, in homes as much as cafes. Ordering it "mazbuu6a" (medium-sweet) is the default when you don't specify, and asking for it "saada" (no sugar) or "7elwe" (sweet) is completely normal too.

exercises.prompt: شو بتحب تشرب؟ (shoo bte7ebb teshrab?)

too_formal.item: أرغب في فنجان من القهوة من فضلك
too_formal.feedback: That's Modern Standard Arabic; nobody says it that way at a cafe table.

exercises.tip: law sama7t / law sama7ti is the everyday word for please.

exercises.prompt: في سكر؟ (fii sukkar?)

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but too stiff for a quick answer across a cafe table.

exercises.tip: halla2 means right now, on the spot.

exercises.prompt: بدي شاي ___ النعناع (biddi shay ___ na3naa3)

too_formal.feedback: That's the MSA preposition ma3a; Damascene fuses bi + al into bl before a consonant.

exercises.tip: bl- attaches directly to the noun, no separate word for 'with'.

exercises.prompt: قهوة ___ (2ahwe ___), meaning medium-sweet coffee

too_formal.feedback: Bookish description; mazbuu6a is the one word everyone actually orders with.

exercises.tip: mazbuu6a literally means 'set right', i.e. just the right amount of sugar.

exercises.prompt: Coffee with no sugar at all.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine MSA, but nobody strings it together this formally in speech.

exercises.tip: khaales at the end means 'at all', it strengthens the negation.

exercises.prompt: I want mint tea.

too_formal.feedback: 'ureed' is correct MSA but sounds like a textbook; biddi is what's actually said.

exercises.tip: biddi is the everyday word for 'I want' in Damascene.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'bitter coffee'?

too_formal.feedback: Overexplained; murra alone does the job in speech.

exercises.tip: murra also means 'bitter' for taste in general.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask 'what would you like to drink?' to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA question form, too formal for a waiter chatting with a customer.

exercises.tip: The -i ending marks you're speaking to a woman.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I like my coffee bitter.

too_formal.feedback: MSA phrasing; the dialect drops the possessive suffix and uses l2ahwe instead.

exercises.tip: murra comes last, describing how you like the coffee.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: A big cup of coffee.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine MSA order but not how it's said casually.

exercises.tip: kbiir (big) comes after the whole noun phrase finjaan 2ahwe.

lessons.title: Reading the Menu

phrases.english: Do you have an English menu?

reply.english: We have fattoush, hummus, and grilled meat.

phrases.english: Is it spicy or not spicy?
What do you recommend I get?
phrases.search_term: waiter recommending a dish to customer

reply.english: Try the mansaf, it's really good.

phrases.english: Is there a dish of the day?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.transliteration: ahleen w sahleen, tfaddalu, haad l menu
dialogue.english: Welcome, please, here's the menu.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: Thanks, but do you have an English menu?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sure, I'll bring it to you now.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: Thank you. What do you recommend we get?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.arabic: المشاوي كتير طيبة هون، وفي طبق اليوم كمان
dialogue.transliteration: l mashaawi ktiir 6ayybe hoon, w fii 6abaq lyoom kaman
dialogue.english: The grilled meat is really good here, and there's also a dish of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.english: What's in the dish of the day?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Maqluba, a little spicy.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: بدي شي خفيف، عندكن أكل نباتي؟
dialogue.english: I want something light, do you have vegetarian food?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sure, we have fattoush, hummus, and tabbouleh.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: منيح، بدي طبق حمص لو سمحت
dialogue.english: Good, I want a plate of hummus please.

response.english: We have fattoush, hummus, and grilled meat.
Try the dish of the day.
Sure, we have hummus and tabbouleh.

lessons.culture: Menus in Damascus often list only Arabic, so asking "3andkon menu bl ingliizi" is a completely normal, non-awkward question. Waiters expect and enjoy being asked "shoo btinsa7ni" (what do you recommend), it's seen as trusting their judgment.

exercises.prompt: شو في عندكن اليوم؟ (shoo fii 3andkon lyoom?)

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA but stiff for a waiter listing today's food out loud.

exercises.tip: 3anna is the dialect word for 'we have'.

exercises.prompt: شو بتنصحني آخد؟ (shoo btinsa7ni aakhod?)

too_formal.item: أنصحك بتجربة المنسف فهو لذيذ جدا
too_formal.feedback: That's a full formal sentence; the dialect answer is short and direct.

exercises.tip: jarreb means 'try it', a casual imperative.

exercises.prompt: قديش ___ هاد؟ (addeesh ___ haad?), asking the price

too_formal.feedback: Overly formal question structure for asking a simple price.

exercises.tip: sa3er means price; addeesh means 'how much'.

exercises.prompt: بدي شي ___ (biddi shi ___), meaning I want something light

too_formal.feedback: Overworded; khafiif alone conveys 'light' in the dialect.

exercises.tip: khafiif describes food that's not heavy.

exercises.prompt: Is there vegetarian food?

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine MSA but not how it's asked casually.

exercises.tip: fii at the start just means 'is there'.

exercises.prompt: What's in this dish?

too_formal.feedback: Sounds like a written question, not something asked at the table.

exercises.tip: haad means 'this' in Damascene, not MSA hatha.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'dessert'?

too_formal.feedback: Just adds an unneeded adjective; 7alawiyyaat alone is the normal word.

exercises.tip: 7alawiyyaat covers sweets and desserts generally.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask for the menu in English?

too_formal.item: هل تمتلكون قائمة طعام باللغة الإنجليزية؟
too_formal.feedback: Way too formal for asking a waiter a quick question.

exercises.tip: bl ingliizi literally means 'in English'.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: What do you have today?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal MSA word order, not the casual dialect flow.

exercises.tip: lyoom (today) comes at the end of the question.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: There is a dish of the day.

too_formal.feedback: yuujad is the MSA word for 'there is'; the dialect just uses fii.

exercises.tip: fii (there is/are) starts the sentence.

lessons.title: Ordering a Meal

phrases.english: I'll have a plate of hummus and fattoush.

phrases.transliteration: haad l6abaq ili w haad ilha
phrases.english: This dish is for me and this is for her.
Can I have a glass of water?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Are you ready to order?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.arabic: إي، بدي آخد طبق حمص وفتوش
dialogue.english: Yes, I'll have a plate of hummus and fattoush.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Okay, and what would you like?

dialogue.speaker: Lama
dialogue.arabic: بدي هاد وهاد، بس بدون بصل لو سمحت
dialogue.transliteration: biddi haad w haad, bas bidoon basal law sama7t
dialogue.english: I want this and this, but without onion please.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Okay, anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.transliteration: mumken ziyaade khobez w kaase mayy?
dialogue.english: Can we have extra bread and a glass of water?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sure, I'll bring it to you now.

dialogue.speaker: Lama
dialogue.arabic: منشان يكون سريع لو سمحت، مستعجلين شوي
dialogue.transliteration: mnshaan ykuun sarii3 law sama7t, musta3jliin shwayy
dialogue.english: Please make it quick, we're a little in a hurry.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: No worries, it'll be ready soon.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.english: Thank you.

pair.english: Do you want onion or without?
Can I have a glass of water?

lessons.culture: Ordering everything at once when the waiter first comes is common, since asking for things one at a time can feel like you're making them run back and forth. Saying "mnshaan ykuun sarii3" is a polite, normal way to signal you're in a hurry without being rude.

exercises.prompt: جاهزين تطلبوا؟ (jaahziin ti6lubu?)

too_formal.feedback: Way too wordy for a one-word yes to the waiter.

exercises.tip: ii is the casual, common word for 'yes' in Damascene.

exercises.prompt: أي شي تاني؟ (ayy shi taani?)

too_formal.feedback: hatha and yakfi are correct MSA but stiffer than the dialect answer.

exercises.tip: heek mnii7 literally means 'like this is good', i.e. that's enough.

exercises.prompt: بدون ___ لو سمحت (bidoon ___ law sama7t), meaning without onion please

too_formal.feedback: Adding 'al-' (the) is grammatically fine MSA but unnecessary in the dialect request.

exercises.tip: basal is onion; bidoon means without.

exercises.prompt: ممكن ___ مي؟ (mumken ___ mayy?), asking for a glass of water

too_formal.feedback: ka2s is the MSA word; kaase is what's used at the table.

exercises.tip: kaase means glass/cup.

exercises.prompt: My order hasn't arrived yet.

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA negation but not how it's phrased at the table.

exercises.tip: lissa means 'still/not yet', paired with ma for the negative.

exercises.prompt: We want the same order.

too_formal.feedback: nureed is correct MSA but biddna is what's actually said.

exercises.tip: biddna is the 'we want' form of biddi.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'extra bread'?

too_formal.feedback: Overworded; ziyaade khobez alone is the normal order phrase.

exercises.tip: ziyaade means 'extra/more'.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask the waiter to repeat the order?

too_formal.item: هل بإمكانك إعادة الطلب من فضلك؟
too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct MSA but a longer, stiffer phrasing.

exercises.tip: mumken is 'can/is it possible', used constantly for polite requests.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Please make it quick.

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA but a different, more formal sentence structure.

exercises.tip: law sama7t (please) comes at the end here.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: This dish is for me and this is for her.
accepted: haad l6abaq ili w haad ilha

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA word order but different possessive forms (li vs ili).

exercises.tip: ili (for me) and ilha (for her) are dialect possessive forms.

lessons.title: Paying the Bill

phrases.english: Do you take cash or card?
Is there a tip included in the bill?
Thanks (lit. wellness of your heart), it was a tasty meal.
Bless your hands, the food was delicious.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: The bill, please.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: I'll bring it right away, one minute.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: How much is the bill?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Twenty-five thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Sana
dialogue.english: Shall we split the bill?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: No, I'm paying today.

dialogue.speaker: Sana
dialogue.arabic: لا، خلينا منقسم، ما في داعي
dialogue.transliteration: la2, khalliina mn2assem, ma fii daa3i
dialogue.english: No, let's split it, there's no need.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Okay, as you like.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Do you take card?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sure, here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Sana
dialogue.arabic: تسلم إيدك، الأكل كان زاكي كتير
dialogue.transliteration: tislam iidak, l2akel kaan zaaki ktiir
dialogue.english: Bless your hands, the food was really delicious.

pair.english: Do you take cash or card?

lessons.culture: Insisting on paying, even after someone offers to split, is a common social dance, expect at least one round of polite refusal before the bill actually gets settled. Saying "tislam iidak" to whoever cooked or served is a warm, genuine way to end the meal, more personal than a plain thank you.

exercises.prompt: قديش الحساب؟ (addeesh l7saab?)

too_formal.item: الفاتورة تبلغ خمسة وعشرين ألف ليرة
too_formal.feedback: Overly formal phrasing for a waiter quoting a price.

exercises.tip: addeesh is the dialect word for 'how much'.

exercises.prompt: بتاخدوا كاش ولا بطاقة؟ (btaakhdu kaash walla be6aa2a?)

too_formal.feedback: kilaahuma is correct MSA but sounds bookish for a quick answer.

exercises.tip: l ethneen means 'the two/both'.

exercises.prompt: خليك بال___ (khalliik bl ___), meaning keep the change

too_formal.feedback: Overworded; baa2i alone covers 'change/remainder'.

exercises.tip: baa2i means 'what remains', i.e. the change.

exercises.prompt: منقسم ال___؟ (mn2assem l ___?), asking to split the bill

too_formal.feedback: faatuura (receipt/invoice) is also used, but not the everyday split-the-bill question.

exercises.tip: 7saab means the bill/account.

exercises.prompt: Is there a tip included in the bill?

too_formal.feedback: ikraamiyye is the MSA word for tip; ba2shiish is what's used in speech.

exercises.tip: ba2shiish is the everyday word for tip.

exercises.prompt: The food was delicious.

too_formal.feedback: lathiith is correct MSA but zaaki is the word actually used casually.

exercises.tip: zaaki means tasty/delicious in the dialect.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'I'm paying'?

too_formal.feedback: sa2aquumu is future-tense MSA, heavier than the direct dialect statement.

exercises.tip: badfa3 is the present/near-future 'I pay' form.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask for the receipt?

too_formal.item: هل يمكنني الحصول على الفاتورة من فضلك؟
too_formal.feedback: Much longer and more formal than the everyday request.

exercises.tip: faatuura is receipt/invoice.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Shall we split the bill?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA question form but a different, more formal opener (hal).

exercises.tip: mn2assem is 'we split', the question mark carries the tone.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Bless your hands, the food was really delicious.
exercises.answer: تسلم إيدك، الأكل كان زاكي كتير
accepted: تسلم إيدك، الأكل كان زاكي كتير
tislam iidak, l2akel kaan zaaki ktiir
تسلم إيدك الأكل كان زاكي كتير

too_formal.item: سلمت يداك، كان الطعام لذيذا جدا
too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA equivalent but stiffer than the warm, casual dialect phrase.

exercises.tip: ktiir (very/really) comes at the end to intensify zaaki.

challenge.title: At the Restaurant
challenge.instructions: Have a full conversation ordering a drink and a meal at a Damascene restaurant, then ask for and settle the bill.
required_elements: Ask what's on the menu or what's recommended
Order at least one drink and one dish, including one preference (e.g. no onion, extra bread, sweet or plain)
Ask for the bill and how much it costs
Say something to close the meal, like a compliment to the food or a thank you
